data.why: A fridge stands cut open in a kitchen; a drink bottle on the shelf is the hook and comes back at the end, and the refrigerant is followed round its loop: the cold coil, the compressor, the hot coils on the back, the thin pipe. The camera opens close on the drink and the ice, then frames each part as it is added, and ends on the hand taking the cold drink.

surprises.claim: The refrigerant R-134a boils at about minus 26 degrees Celsius at normal air pressure.

surprises.claim: A fridge compressor squeezes the refrigerant gas, which makes it hot; the condenser coils on the back release that heat into the kitchen.
surprises.search: refrigerator compressor hot gas condenser coils release heat into kitchen

surprises.claim: A capillary tube or expansion valve drops the refrigerant's pressure so it can boil and cool in the evaporator.

ideas.idea: a drink and ice in a box is a fridge
the ice melts and the drink warms
a coil of refrigerant that boils at minus 26 degrees soaks up heat
once it has all boiled to gas the coil stops cooling
a compressor pumps the gas round and squeezes it
condenser coils on the back shed the heat and the gas turns liquid
the liquid is still under pressure and cannot boil in the coil
a thin pipe drops the pressure so it boils and frosts the coil again
it never stops cooling and the drink freezes
a thermostat stops the compressor when it is cold enough
reach in for an ice-cold drink

sentences.text: If you chill a drink with ice in a box, you have a fridge.
But the ice melts, and the drink warms up.
So you add a coil where cold liquid boils at minus 26 degrees.
But soon the coil holds only gas and stops cooling.
So a compressor pumps the gas round and squeezes it.
But the squeezed gas comes out burning hot.
So coils on the back shed that heat.
But that cooled liquid stays squeezed and cannot boil.
So a thin pipe drops the pressure, and it frosts.
But the frost never stops, and the drink freezes.
So a thermostat stops the compressor when it's cold.
Reach in, and grab an ice-cold drink.
